title: MOE routing, ROPE scaling & KV-shard tuning for on-prem inference
summary: Deep technical session to scope an on-prem pilot: measure MOE routing cost with token affinity, evaluate ROPE decay effects for 64k contexts on Llama/Mistral/Qwen variants, and design KV-shard strategy to keep tail latency under 200ms. Redwood to run targeted benchmarks and provide a tuning guide and config artifacts.
action_items: Priya Raman: run KV-shard 8-node benchmark using customer's 16k sequence traces and report p95/p99 by 2026-07-15
Marco Ruiz: provide a sanitized 24-hour trace and target latency SLO doc by 2026-07-12
Jamie Lawson: share on-prem checklist and security packaging + SOC2 summary by 2026-07-10
Oscar Li: deliver initial quantization profile recommendations and a small repro for the Qwen-14B finetuned routing case by 2026-07-18
next_steps: Schedule hands-on benchmark run (Redwood SE on customer's onprem cluster)
Follow-up call w/ results week of 2026-07-20
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08 09:32 UTC
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Lawson (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Oscar Li (Redwood SE), Nina Torres (Redwood CSM), Ellen Park (BlueHarbor HoML), Marco Ruiz (Platform), Tara Singh (SRE), Dmitri Kozlov (Research)

[00:00] Jamie Lawson: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro — i'm jamie, i'm the AE on the account. we'll let priya and oscar lead most of the tech deep dive. nina here for follow-ups. could we do quick roll call?

[00:18] Ellen Park: Ellen here. excited, we've been wrestling with long context tuning and the MoE cost swings.

[00:25] Marco Ruiz: Marco, platform. we manage the onprem k8s cluster and the storage side.

[00:32] Tara Singh: Tara, SRE - availability and latency are the main concerns for us.

[00:40] Priya Raman: cool. goal for today: outline a benchmark plan for MOE routing cost with token-affinity, dig into ROPE scaling issues for 32k-64k contexts, and propose a KV-cache sharding topology that keeps tail latencies reasonable.

[01:05] Dmitri Kozlov: quick note: we've got a couple of 24h traces and a few synthetic 64k sessions. we'll share. some of our models are Llama-13B variants, a Mistral-7B large med config, and a Qwen-14B-like architecture with an MoE head.

[01:30] Oscar Li: got it. first thing — MOE routing costs. the big hidden is token affinity: if you have sequences that gravitate to a small set of experts, routing ends up concentrating on a few GPUs and you lose parallelism and increase p99. we usually measure three things: tokens-per-expert distribution, pct of sequential hot runs, and cross-host bandwidth during expert-allreduce.

[01:58] Marco Ruiz: that matches what we saw — about 70% of tokens went to 2 experts in some workloads. latency spiked when microbatching kicked in.

[02:13] Priya Raman: right. mitigation patterns: adaptive capacity factoring, adding stochastic routing noise, and token-level load-balancing in the router. for onprem, we can do two options: 1) change routing top-k for the router at runtime, or 2) split the model across more expert shards and accept slightly higher model footprint. both have cost/latency tradeoffs.

[02:44] Ellen Park: can you quantify the hit if we increase expert count from 16 to 32? we have capacity to add nodes but want to understand throughput vs cost.

[02:53] Priya Raman: in our tests, going 16->32 experts with the same total params reduces per-expert token pressure by roughly 35-45% and p99 improved by ~22% on balanced traces. but cold-start and KV-cache warmup can increase initial latency. so you need a warmup plan.

[03:20] Tara Singh: warmup how — prefill KV cache for likely prefixes? we can't pre-warm for all tokens.

[03:28] Oscar Li: you prefill with top-k prefixes derived from traces. and you use a TTL-based prefetched KV per-shard. we also recommend sticky routing window — keep some affinity for short windows so the cache hits. that reduces cross-shard fetches.

[03:50] Dmitri Kozlov: question about ROPE/positional decay — at 32k to 64k context we see generation quality drop and some hallucination spikes. is that expected?

[04:03] Priya Raman: yes, ROPE scaling and numerical decay are common. different architectures handle extrapolation differently — Mistral variants tend to be slightly more robust up to 32k with linear pos bias adjustments, Qwen variants sometimes need explicit rope re-scaling or rotary decay compensation patch. Llama-derivatives vary by tokenizer and position embedding handling.

[04:30] Marco Ruiz: any quick knobs to try? we need something we can deploy fast.

[04:35] Priya Raman: three fast knobs: 1) position-scaling factor (rope alpha) slightly >1 for longer contexts; 2) chunked attention window with overlap + offline KV stitching; 3) lower temperature for long-range generation to reduce hallucination. the position-scaling is cheap; patch can be toggled in runtime config.

[05:05] Ellen Park: is that safe for all models or do we need model-specific patches?

[05:12] Oscar Li: model-specific. Mistral responded well to alpha=1.05 in our pretests; Qwen needed 1.12 for 64k but quality tradeoffs happened. so we recommend per-model validation sets. we'll provide a small matrix test.

[05:33] Jamie Lawson: quick interjection — security/compliance questions came up upstream: we need to outline the network layout for KV shards and ensure data-at-rest encryption on the shards; BlueHarbor wanted KMS + HSM options.

[05:48] Tara Singh: yes, show us the encryption story and RBAC. we can't have plain text KV blobs on disk.

[05:54] Priya Raman: understood. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and optional on-disk encryption for KV caches. for onprem we provide an operator that mounts encrypted volumes with your keys. we'll send the SOC2 + encryption runbook.

[06:12] Marco Ruiz: good. now microbatching: our latency SLO is 200ms for interactive agents, but throughput targets are high. how do you pick microbatch windows to balance CPU/GPU utilization vs p99?

[06:26] Oscar Li: typical approach: set an adaptive batching window keyed by route. for routes tagged low-latency, set max batch size = 4 and max wait = 8ms; for high-throughput routes, let batch size grow and wait up to 40-50ms. we also recommend continuous batching for KV-heavy workloads to amortize kernel launches.

[06:53] Tara Singh: 8ms wait — is that realistic in our env? our network tail is about 3-5ms sometimes.

[07:00] Priya Raman: it's a guideline. you should calibrate per rack/zone. we can run an automated calibration job (Redwood tool) on your cluster to map optimal windows.

[07:15] Dmitri Kozlov: about KV-shard topology — is it better to shard by key hash or by token-range for sequence-affinity workloads?

[07:25] Priya Raman: token-range sharding aligns with sequence locality but can create hot shards. key-hash evens load globally but destroys locality. we recommend a hybrid: range-shard for recent prefixes (hot range), hash-evict to overflow buckets. implement a two-tier routing table: hot-range -> preferred shard, else hashed fallback.

[07:50] Marco Ruiz: that seems complex operationally. we'd prefer something simpler to start.

[07:56] Oscar Li: start with simple hash-shard with a small LRU on each shard and collect telemetry. if you see hotspotting, promote frequent prefixes into a hot-range table. the telemetry is key: tokens-per-key, remote fetch rates, and cross-shard fetchs.

[08:20] Ellen Park: what about cross-host bandwidth during re-shard or scale events? we can't saturate our interconnect.

[08:28] Priya Raman: avoid full re-shards in production. use consistent hashing with bounded-staleness routing tables and background rebalancer that migrates hot keys gradually. we also recommend compressing KV payloads and using delta updates where possible.

[08:45] Jamie Lawson: can we talk about quantization? Ellen, you mentioned you're experimenting with 4-bit. What's your constraint?

[08:52] Ellen Park: yes, we're running 4-bit QAT on some Mistral forks to save memory. but we've seen routing instability when weights are in 4-bit and router logits go noisy.

[09:05] Oscar Li: that tracks. quantization can change the softmax sharpness of routing logits. we use small FP16 or mixed-precision router compute even when body weights are quantized. maintain router in FP16, or use a tiny FP32 head for router scoring. that preserves routing stability.

[09:26] Priya Raman: also consider per-token calibration. on hot tokens, prefer higher precision; for tail tokens, allow more quant error. Redwood's runtime supports precision hints per-op.

[09:40] Marco Ruiz: operationally, can we keep two images — quantized model and a higher-precision router image — or is that too heavy?

[09:50] Oscar Li: you can keep a mixed image: body in 4-bit, router and gating in fp16. memory overhead is tiny for the router. it's better than tandem images.

[10:05] Dmitri Kozlov: we have a concern: when an expert 'blows up' — i.e., it gets hotspot and OOMs — how does Redwood handle graceful degradation?

[10:16] Priya Raman: Redwood has fallback policies: if an expert fails, router can fallback to top-k-1 routing and redistribute tokens with a soft penalty. we also support capacity-factor throttling where tokens get probabilistically dropped to cheaper dense model fallback. we'll show the policy config.

[10:40] Jamie Lawson: let's review an example run: Marco, can you summarize current infra — GPU types, interconnect?

[10:47] Marco Ruiz: we have 8 nodes, each with 8xH100s, Mellanox 200Gb/s, and NVMe pools. we can allocate up to 32 GPUs for a pilot. network latencies within rack are 60-120us. cross-rack 400-800us.

[11:10] Priya Raman: great. that's high bandwidth — good for MoE. for KV shard sizing on that infra, recommended shard per NVMe local to node with replica=2 for availability and an async background checkpoint. avoid sync cross-host writes on hot paths.

[11:30] Ellen Park: checkpoint frequency? we want to recover without long warmups.

[11:34] Oscar Li: checkpoint every 5 minutes with incremental snapshots; full snapshot nightly. smaller incremental checkpoints reduce warmup time. also keep a lightweight population map persisted to rebuild hot hotspots quickly.

[11:50] Dmitri Kozlov: another question — how to measure effective ROPE decay in our traces? what metric do you use to decide when to apply scaling?

[11:57] Priya Raman: we compute positional-correlation drop: take perplexity or next-token loss as a function of position for a held-out set; when slope increases beyond threshold at long positions, mark as decay. we also run KL divergence between short-context and long-context distributions. we'll provide the analysis script.

[12:20] Marco Ruiz: are there known model forks where ROPE is fixed upstream? we don't want to fork model code too much.

[12:26] Priya Raman: some Qwen forks include a rope-fix patch. Llama community has a couple of PRs for scaled rotary. Mistral less so; we patch at runtime more often. we'll list model-specific changelogs in the runbook.

[12:45] Jamie Lawson: ok long list. let's be pragmatic — propose a pilot plan: Redwood runs benchmark on your traces with three axes: routing config (top-k, capacity), rope-scaling alpha, and KV-shard topology (hash vs hybrid). collect p50/p95/p99, engineering ops cost, and token-cost estimate.

[13:08] Ellen Park: timeline?

[13:10] Jamie Lawson: we can run an initial job this week if Marco shares traces. full runs will be next week. PRiya, Oscar — you good to own the runs?

[13:20] Priya Raman: yes. we'll run parallel tests for Llama-13B, Mistral-7B-large, and Qwen-14B-like. we'll also include a version with router in FP16 + body in 4-bit.

[13:35] Marco Ruiz: I'll sanitize and upload a 24h trace by Monday 2026-07-12.

[13:40] Tara Singh: we'll want to review the security packaging before any onprem agent is installed.

[13:46] Nina Torres: we'll share the SOC2 summary and encryption runbook by Friday 2026-07-10. also linking to the quickstart: https://redwood.ai/onprem/quickstart

[13:58] Oscar Li: notes on instrumentation: we'll need to instrument tokens-per-expert, cross-shard remote fetch ratio, per-shard KV hit rate, and per-request end-to-end time broken down by kernel vs transfer. Redwood will provide the grafana dashboards and a prometheus exporter.

[14:20] Dmitri Kozlov: curious — what's the expected cost delta between hosted Redwood API and doing this onprem pilot? our finance wants rough numbers.

[14:30] Jamie Lawson: ballpark: hosted for similar throughput was ~1.6x the infra marginal cost because we amortize ops; onprem fixed cost can be lower per-token but you pay for ops and cold start risk. we'll produce a cost comparison using your cluster numbers.

[14:48] Ellen Park: any red flags we missed?

[14:52] Priya Raman: watch for hotspotting tied to user-id affinity and long-tail prefixes — that's a common surprise. Also monitor router entropy; if it's too low, plan to increase expert count or add stochastic routing.

[15:10] Marco Ruiz: got it. can you also document the fallback behaviors and the A/B rollout pattern for routing changes? we want rollbacks to be automated.

[15:20] Oscar Li: yes, Redwood's rollout supports canary on fraction of traffic, automatic rollback on latency or error budget breach, and shadow routing for validation. we'll attach sample configs.

[15:35] Jamie Lawson: wrap-up: recap next steps and owners. Marco to upload traces by 2026-07-12; Priya/Oscar to run benchmarks and deliver results week of 2026-07-20; Jamie to share SOC2/encryption doc by 2026-07-10; Oscar to share quant guidance by 2026-07-18.

[16:00] Ellen Park: thank you, this was super helpful.

[16:05] Tara Singh: thanks everyone.

[16:10] Jamie Lawson: all right, we'll follow up in email with the runbook and a calendar invite for the results review.
